item.title: ‘The hand of god’ and all that: Lineker, Shilton et al look back at 1986 England-Argentina clash – The Match review
item.description:
Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict

Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century, that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous cheating; what could they do in the face of such authentic genius?

Over and above football matters, it’s clear to see that there were bigger things at stake. Rather obviously, it happened only four years after the Falklands war, which thoroughly poisoned already tense relations between Britain and Argentina. The Match situates the 1986 clash as part of a continuum of strife, dating back at least to the arrival in 1765 of a British sea captain, John Byron, on the Falklands to claim them for Britain. Other key moments: Argentina’s Antonio Rattín getting sent off during the 1966 World Cup, and Maradona being invited on stage by Queen to sing Another One Bites the Dust during their mammoth 1981 South American tour.

item.title: Colombia to euthanise hippos for the first time: ten animals in four months

item.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
item.description:
Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

item.title: The Quechua rapper and an artistic movement reclaiming language of the Incas
item.description:
Renata Flores has gained global recognition for her music in Indigenous language whose speakers have faced social stigma

With her long black hair braided into beaded plaits, a delicate silver nose ring, and intricately patterned Andean textile draped around her chest above baggy, low-riding jeans, Renata Flores is a visual reflection of her music: a fusion of traditional and transgressive, old and new, rural and urban.

Nicknamed the “queen of Quechua rap”, Flores, 25, has earned global recognition for mixing Peru’s main Indigenous language and Andean instruments with the urban beats of trap, rap, hip-hop and reggaeton.
